families.s: HSE maintenance priorities for catering equipment and premises
families.t: routine checks, planned maintenance, breakdown work, inspections, tests, slips, heat, electricity, fire, gas and machinery
f: Poor maintenance is an important underlying cause of catering accidents.
Maintenance planning should address slips, hot or harmful substances, electrical injury, fire, explosion and machinery hazards.
Routine user checks can identify obvious deterioration and defects.
Planned preventive maintenance should be scheduled before equipment becomes unsafe.
Breakdown maintenance requires a safe system and appropriate isolation.
Inspection, examination and testing should match equipment and legal requirements.
Cleaning is part of maintenance where grease, debris or contamination affects safety.
Defects should be reported, prioritised and kept out of service where continued use would be unsafe.
families.g: Catering-maintenance risk depends on equipment and deterioration, defect severity, cleaning and access, energy and isolation, contractor competence, inspection frequency, records and return-to-service control.

families.s: HSE safe use of cleaning substances in hospitality
families.t: detergents, rinse aids, drain and oven cleaners, disinfectants, toilet cleaners, bleach, sanitisers, descalers, storage, mixing and PPE
f: Hospitality cleaning can involve washing-up liquids, dishwasher detergents and rinse aids.
Drain cleaners and oven cleaners can cause serious burns or eye injury.
Disinfectants, toilet cleaners, bleach, sanitisers and descalers require assessed controls.
Employers should identify the hazards and prevent or adequately control exposure.
Products should be stored securely and kept in correctly labelled containers.
Incompatible chemicals should not be mixed because hazardous reactions or gases can result.
Dosing and dilution systems can reduce handling of concentrates.
Gloves, eye protection, ventilation, spill response and training should match the substance and task.
families.g: Hospitality chemical risk depends on product and concentration, dilution and mixing, spray and splash, storage and compatibility, ventilation, contact duration, PPE, training and emergency response.

families.t: risk assessment, clients, workers and public, slips, skin, MSDs, work at height, chemicals, equipment, communication and supervision
f: Cleaning businesses must manage risks to cleaners and other people affected by the work.
Common cleaning risks include slips, skin disease, musculoskeletal disorders and work at height.
Cleaning can also create hazards for occupants and members of the public using the area.
Risk assessment should cover all cleaning tasks, loads, workers and work environments.
Restricted space, time pressure and poorly designed equipment can increase risk.
Communication is needed between cleaning contractors, clients and product or equipment suppliers.
Equipment and work methods should be selected to reduce exposure and physical effort.
Arrangements should be reviewed when premises, schedules, chemicals, machines or client activities change.
families.g: Cleaning risk depends on premises and occupants, task and timing, contaminants and chemicals, equipment and maintenance, physical demands, work at height, communication and supervision.

families.s: HSE slips-and-trips prevention in cleaning work
families.t: wet floors, trailing cables, cleaning method, access control, signage, communication, flooring, footwear and effectiveness checks
f: Cleaning can create slip and trip hazards for cleaners and people entering the work area.
Smooth floors left damp can become slippery.
Vacuum and floor-machine cables can create trip hazards.
A cleaning management system should identify problem areas and suitable controls.
Cleaning method, chemical and equipment should suit the contaminant and floor.
Communication should prevent people entering areas while unsafe conditions remain.
Controls should include prompt treatment of spills and management of obstructions.
The organisation should check that the cleaning regime is actually reducing slip risk.
families.g: Cleaning slip risk depends on floor and contaminant, cleaning method and drying, cable and equipment layout, access and timing, footwear, lighting, communication and monitoring.

families.t: wet work, cleaning products, avoidance, gloves, hand drying, moisturising, skin checks, reporting and training
f: Cleaning workers can develop work-related contact dermatitis from wet work and cleaning products.
Employers should assess the risk and provide adequate controls, information and training.
Contact should be avoided where possible by using handled tools rather than direct hand cleaning.
Suitable gloves should be selected for the product and task.
Hands should be dried thoroughly after washing.
Moisturisers help replenish skin oils and support the skin barrier.
Workers should check for itchy, dry or red skin and report early symptoms.
Early detection and control review can prevent minor skin damage becoming severe occupational dermatitis.
families.g: Cleaning dermatitis risk depends on wet-work frequency, product hazard, direct contact and immersion, glove material and duration, hand care, skin susceptibility, training and surveillance.
